generatedProse.concept-context: In any subject, a presentation is a common form of assessment. You might present a piece of reading, a small study of your own, or a poster at a conference-style session. Whatever the discipline, the point is the same: you communicate an argument or set of findings clearly to an audience, usually with slides. A presentation builds the academic voice a subject values, and the clear communication that study and professional work both demand.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students given the same brief: a ten-minute presentation on a topic from their module.

Student A treats the task as reading out information. The notes go straight onto the slides, to be read aloud line by line, covering everything that was found. The material is there, but the audience is left reading dense slides while Student A reads the same words. This is really a document read out, not a talk, and it misses what a presentation is for.

Student B treats the task as communicating a point to an audience. Student B works out one clear message, chooses what the audience needs to hear, and uses the slides to support the spoken argument rather than carry it. The talk has a shape and a purpose. This is what an academic presentation is: a spoken argument, made clearly to listeners.

Both students had the same brief. Only Student B understood that a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud.
generatedProse.summary: An academic presentation is a spoken piece of assessed work in which you communicate an argument or findings to an audience, usually with slides. It builds your academic voice and transferable skills such as clear communication. You can now explain what a presentation is, give an example of a skill it builds, and recognise the main types used for assessment. The next lessons turn this into practice: how you plan and structure a presentation, and how you design its visual aids.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Student B understand that Student A did not?

items.text: That a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud.
That more slides always make a presentation better.
That the material should be covered as quickly as possible.
That reading notes aloud word for word is the safest approach.

feedback.correct: That's right. Student B understood a presentation is communication to an audience.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Student B grasped about the purpose of a presentation.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Student B understood a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud. The other options mistake slides, speed or reciting for the point.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
